title: "Power Lines: batch size, weight decay and long-horizon training"
subtitle: "AdamW timescales, optimal versus critical batch and a replication protocol"
date: 2026-11-02

## Why this paper matters for our overtrained model

[Bergsma et al., Power Lines v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13738v2) studies AdamW weight decay and batch scaling across model size and training horizon, including heavily overtrained settings up to1,280 TPP. It makes a LR/batch-only tuning plan incomplete: weight decay interacts with both. Primary artifacts are the [PDF](../../references/optimization/2025-power-lines-batch-size-weight-decay/paper.pdf) and [LaTeX/code metadata](../../references/optimization/2025-power-lines-batch-size-weight-decay/metadata.json).

The reported experiments use Cerebras CS-3, SlimPajama, a GPT-like ALiBi/SwiGLU family, AdamW/μP and a fixed1.1B-token validation set. The schedule is linear decay with 10% warmup. This is close to our **overtraining regime**, not our exact hardware, model, corpus or schedule.

## 1. Derive the timescale before applying its fit

Ignoring the gradient term momentarily, decoupled AdamW decay contributes

$$
W_{s+1}\approx(1-\eta\lambda)W_s.
$$

At approximately constant peak LR $\eta$ and decay $\lambda$, its update-count timescale is $1/(\eta\lambda)$. With $S=D/B_t$ updates over horizon $D$ and token batch $B_t$, the normalized timescale is

$$
\tau=\frac{1/(\eta\lambda)}{D/B_t}
=\frac{B_t}{\eta\lambda D}.
$$

During annealing the instantaneous value changes. The paper evaluates the nominal timescale at peak LR under matched schedule shapes; it is not claiming the LR is actually constant for the whole run. Group-wise actual LR/decay values matter under μP. A base LR printed in a config may not be the LR used by each hidden weight.

## 2. What the weight-decay sweeps find

At fixed $N,D$, increasing batch while preserving the tuned timescale can require changing decay. The paper then finds that optimal normalized timescale varies with tokens per parameter:

$$
\tau_\star\approx1.084(D/N)^{-0.527},\qquad
\lambda_\star=\frac{B_t}{\eta D\tau_\star}.
$$

This is empirical across the studied family. It corrects an unconditional “keep $\tau$ constant as everything scales” rule. It also gives a practical alternative to repeatedly changing LR when horizon or batch changes: tune decay/timescale on small cells, fit its TPP dependence, and validate at larger scale.

Concrete evidence (§2.4): a 111M/200TPP example obtains held-out losses 2.810 with default HPs, 2.808 after LR tuning and 2.805 after decay tuning. Table 1 compares tuning decay versus LR at 610M/20TPP across batches; decay tuning is superior in six of eight comparisons. These are small but controlled differences, not proof of a universal decay optimum.

The paper reports a strong timescale power-law fit and additional held-out scale checks. That supports testing the prescription in our setup. It does not justify inserting its decay value into MuonH: Hyperball matrices use a different norm constraint, and some scalar groups may still have separate decay.

## 3. Optimal and critical batch answer different questions

**Loss-optimal batch** $B_\star(N,D)$ minimizes final loss for fixed model and token horizon. **Critical batch** describes diminishing returns from increasing data parallelism at a specified target loss.

If $D(B)$ tokens and $S(B)$ updates reach target loss, the paper uses the McCandlish-style tradeoff

$$
\left(\frac{S}{S_{\min}}-1\right)
\left(\frac{D}{D_{\min}}-1\right)=1,
\qquad B_{\rm crit}=D_{\min}/S_{\min}.
$$

Since $B=D/S$, this implies $D=D_{\min}(1+B/B_{\rm crit})$ and $S=S_{\min}(1+B_{\rm crit}/B)$ under this fitted relation. Small batches need many updates but little extra data; large batches reduce steps with diminishing returns and increasing token demand. This mathematical interpretation does not by itself determine fastest wall time on a specific cluster.

## 4. The coefficient units are easy to get wrong

Figure 1 reports

$$
B_{\star,s}=0.0306D^{0.383},\qquad
B_{{\rm crit},s}=0.0471D_{\min}^{0.462}.
$$

**The outputs here are sequences of length 2,048; $D$ and $D_{\min}$ are tokens.** Multiply by2,048 for token batches. In the timescale equation, use $B_t$ in tokens. AppendixE explicitly distinguishes these conventions.

The exponents imply that quadrupling horizon raises fitted loss-optimal sequence batch by about 1.70; the corresponding critical-batch expression grows by about 1.90 when its $D_{\min}$ increases fourfold. These are consequences of the fitted equations, not new experiment observations.

Changing context length means rechecking packing/attention cost and the relevant batch conventions; a sequence-batch coefficient is not portable by changing the sequence-length field alone. Likewise, a model-size label that includes embeddings in our plan can differ from the paper's parameter convention.

## 5. μP does not remove horizon and decay tuning

μP aims to preserve useful width transfer through coordinated initialization, parameter-group LR and other rules. The paper distinguishes base LR from actual scaled LR. Its results show why a width-transferred LR is not the entire training recipe: batch and decay still interact with token horizon.

Do not summarize μP as “divide every LR by width.” Implement and inspect each group. Depth changes, MoE routing and expert-bank normalization need their own tests. Marin's AdamH/MuonH prescriptions differ from AdamW/μP, so compare fully tuned algorithms instead of combining their coefficients.

## Our replication and adaptation protocol

1. Recreate a small standard dense or transparent MoE reference with documented μP/group semantics, tokenizer, corpus and schedule. For a faithful paper replication, match its family/data and context before extending it.
2. At a reference $(N,D)$, sweep several feasible token batches and decay values while holding the peak-LR prescription fixed. Check instability and whether minima are bracketed.
3. Repeat at independent horizons near the intended overtraining range, including 200+TPP under a declared count convention. Convert every trial to $\tau$ using actual LR/decay and token batch.
4. Fit $\log\tau=a+b\log(D/N)$, then validate decay predictions at unseen size/horizon with local LR and decay brackets. Compare with a constant-decay baseline given equal tuning effort.
5. To estimate critical batch, train enough trajectories across batches to interpolate tokens/updates required for common **held-out target losses**. Do not call the fastest throughput setting a statistical critical batch.
6. Profile wall time versus token batch and accumulation on our actual GPU topology. Choose on a quality/runtime frontier, not a coefficient alone.
7. Add cyber data only after a baseline is qualified; run selected transfer cells before deciding whether new coefficients are needed.

For repeated data, record unique bucket pools and cumulative epochs separately from $D$. A long-horizon law fit on diverse fresh text may not describe memorizing a tiny repeated corpus. For our MoE candidate, total stored TPP, active TPP and executed compute each need explicit reporting.

The [Marin tuning guide](../optimizers/marin-hyperparameter-search.qmd) integrates these checks into a staged grid/adaptive search. The paper supplies evidence for including decay/timescale; it does not select our hero optimizer or promise a universal long-horizon coefficient.
